extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and readers of literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Lecture-style guidance on distinguishing and creating major 'aspects' of the novel (fantasy, parody/adaptation, prophetic fiction), with practical and critical criteria for handling mythology, tone, character-extension, realism, and endings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantasist's blending of magic and common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The mark of the true fantasist is to 'merge the kingdoms of magic and common sense by using words that apply to both.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use language and images that function plausibly in both the ordinary and the supernatural realms so the mixture 'comes alive.' Example: Norman Matson's use of words that apply to both worlds creates a lively blend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mythology and supernatural devices (in fantasy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythology is central to fantasy; the fantasist borrows or creates supernatural 'machines' and mythic elements as the work's machinery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ supernatural devices sparingly and appropriately — an ill-placed device can make the fantasy 'heavy or thin.' Example: in Zuleika Dobson some invented machines sustain the mythology, but entrusting the heroine to certain devices would be inept. Smooth transitions between mythologies are necessary to uphold tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixture of realism, wit, charm and mythology (fantasy tone)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful fantasy often treats a theme 'with a mixture of realism, wittiness, charm and mythology,' where mythology is most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for 'freedom of invocation' and an iridescent yet profound tone; be cautious of endings which can cause the book to 'flag' if tone or treatment collapses at the close.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody/adaptation as a structural device
rubrics_metrics.description: The fantasist may 'adopt for his mythology some earlier work and use it as a framework or quarry for his own purposes' (parody or adaptation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parody/adaptation can jumpstart writers who struggle to invent characters or worlds by providing patterns and cornices to hang new material on. Beware false starts (Fielding's Joseph Andrews) and use the source-mythology in ways that genuinely serve your aims. Examples: The Magic Flute (Lowes Dickinson), Ulysses (Joyce using the Odyssey).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophecy as a tone of voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophecy (as an aspect of the novel) is primarily 'a tone of voice' — an accent or song in the novelist's phrase that implies vast beliefs or visions rather than merely foretelling the future.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on the novelist's state of mind and the actual words used; prophecy filters particular world-views into the turns of phrase. The novelist will often neglect ordinary 'furniture' (tables and chairs) because the accent of song displaces common-sense focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader qualities required for prophetic fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction 'demands two qualities: humility and the suspension of the sense of humour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers must adopt humility to hear the prophet's voice and lay aside immediate laughter (which would reduce the prophet to a figure of fun). Without these reader dispositions, prophetic tones will be misread or dismissed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters' capacity for extension to universality (prophetic extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: In prophetic fiction characters 'stand for more than themselves' — they 'expand to embrace' infinity and thereby imply universal significance beyond their individual lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether characters imply something beyond their concrete situation (Dostoevsky's Mitya, Alyosha) rather than remaining strictly bounded personalities (George Eliot's Hetty). Prophetic characters invite readers to share deeper emotions and sensations that reach back into universal experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermittent/spasmodic realism
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic novels are 'spasmodically realistic' — they can be 'patiently accurate' about ordinary details at moments while otherwise giving over to song or vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use precise, often meticulous description in intermissions of prophecy (trials, staircases, cataloguing) to anchor the reader; this 'intermittent realism' creates a rough, dented surface that later smooths into lasting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophetic voice: song not reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophet's method 'gives us the sensation of a song or of sound' and 'does not reflect' or 'hammer away.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for lyric, tonal, and songlike phrasing rather than philosophic reflection or didactic repetition. Beware of 'talk' or overworked analytic method (the lecture excludes Joyce for being too talky/workmanlike).

rubrics_metrics.name: Orientation toward unity vs multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Prophetic fiction's 'face is towards unity' while fantasy 'glances about'; confusion in prophecy is incidental, in fantasy it is fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether your work seeks a unifying vision (prophecy) or a playful, shifting multiplicity of mythologies and confused perspectives (fantasy). This determines coherence, structure, and what counts as success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk/reward of prophetic distortion of realism
rubrics_metrics.description: The prophet 'may smash or distort' domestic furniture (ordinary realism) but may also 'illumine' objects, rendering them more vivid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept occasional breaking of common-sense coherence as a trade-off for heightened illumination; the prophetic writer manipulates a 'beam of light' that makes mundane objects exceptional — expect roughness of surface and intermittent dislocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and ending maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Endings are often 'dreadful' and 'fatal to fiction' if they fail to maintain the chosen aspect (fantastic or prophetic) of the book; a closing scene must preserve the book's spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard the close: maintain the established mixture of tone, mythology, and treatment so the ending does not 'flag' or become 'almost nasty' at close quarters (example: criticisms of some endings in Zuleika Dobson).
